findings.title: Caller-supplied options.signal is silently discarded (regression in cancellation contract)
findings.evidence: Spread of options followed by an unconditional signal override: 'const response = await fetch(url, { ...options, signal: controller.signal });'. Previously options were forwarded untouched, so 'fetchJson(url, { signal })' allowed the caller to cancel; now the internal controller's signal replaces the caller's, and nothing ever calls abort on it on the caller's behalf. Reachable path: any call site doing 'fetchJson(url, { signal: myAbortController.signal })' then 'myAbortController.abort()' will no longer cancel the request, and the caller has no way to stop a request early (only the fixed timeout ends it).
findings.evidence_quote: const response = await fetch(url, { ...options, signal: controller.signal });
findings.recommendation: Compose signals instead of overwriting: accept the caller signal, keep it, and either forward it via 'AbortSignal.any([controller.signal, options.signal])' (Node 20+/modern browsers) or attach a listener that calls controller.abort(reason) when the caller signal aborts; document the behaviour and add a test covering caller-initiated abort.

findings.title: timeoutMs is unvalidated; 0/null/NaN abort immediately and Infinity has no safe meaning
findings.evidence: 'const timer = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), timeoutMs);' is called with whatever the caller passes. 'timeoutMs: null' or NaN are coerced to a 0ms delay so every request aborts immediately, and there is no supported way to opt out of the timeout: passing Infinity hits Node's TimeoutOverflowWarning path (delay clamped to ~1ms), i.e. the opposite of 'no timeout'. Reachable: 'fetchJson(url, { timeoutMs: null })' from config/env parsing.
findings.recommendation: Validate/normalise timeoutMs (reject or clamp non-finite/negative/non-number values, or treat 0/Infinity explicitly as no timeout) and add a guard so a misconfigured value cannot turn every request into an instant abort.

findings.title: No test asserts the timeout actually aborts, or that the timer is cleared
findings.evidence: 'const controller = new AbortController();' plus the finally block are the whole abort mechanism, and no test command was run for this change; the two risky behaviours (abort fires after timeoutMs with a non-2xx-free rejection, and clearTimeout prevents a dangling timer after success/failure) are both unverified.
findings.recommendation: Add tests: (a) a request slower than timeoutMs rejects with the abort error and not a generic failure, (b) a fast successful request clears the timer (e.g. assert process/timer handles are clean or spy on clearTimeout), (c) a non-2xx fast response still throws the request-failed error.

findings.title: Passing null as the second argument now throws instead of being forwarded
findings.evidence: The parameter is destructured with a default: 'export async function fetchJson(url, { timeoutMs = 8000, ...options } = {}) {' — a default only applies to undefined, so 'fetchJson(url, null)' now throws a TypeError where the previous signature forwarded null to fetch (which treats it as no init). Low impact unless a call site passes null; also the abort rejection is an unlabelled AbortError, so callers cannot tell a timeout from any other abort.
findings.recommendation: Normalise the argument ('options ?? {}') if null forwarding matters, and wrap the abort rejection in an Error that states the URL and timeoutMs so timeout failures are distinguishable from other fetch errors.
